title: JWST Reveals a Planet Where Rock Clouds Form and Vanish Daily
summary: Imagine a world where the morning sky fills with clouds made not of water, but of rock. That's exactly what astronomers have discovered on WASP-94A b, a gas giant located nearly 700 light-years away in the constellation Microscopium. Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), scientists observed a dramatic daily weather cycle: clouds of magnesium silicate condense on the planet's morning side and evaporate by evening. The findings, published in Science, mark one of the first direct observations of cloud cycling on a hot Jupiter—a class of exoplanets that orbit perilously close to their stars. WASP-94A b is tidally locked, meaning one hemisphere permanently faces its star, reaching temperatures over 1,000 degrees Celsius. As the planet rotates, the morning side brings cooler air from the night side into the blazing day side, causing minerals to condense into clouds. On the evening side, these clouds vanish. "It was a huge surprise," said David Sing, a Bloomberg Distinguished Professor at Johns Hopkins and co-author of the study. "We saw a real dichotomy between the weather on both sides of the planet, and huge differences in cloud coverage." The team used a clever technique: as the planet transited its star, JWST separately examined the leading edge (morning) and trailing edge (evening). The morning side was thick with clouds, while the evening side was almost clear. This clarity allowed scientists to directly study the atmosphere without the cloudy interference that plagued earlier telescopes like Hubble. "With Hubble, we got an average view of the whole planet with data from the clouds and the atmosphere squished together," explained lead author Sagnick Mukherjee, a postdoctoral fellow at Arizona State University. "This approach with JWST lets us localize our observations." The clearer data also solved a long-standing puzzle: previous measurements suggested WASP-94A b had hundreds of times more oxygen and carbon than Jupiter, challenging planet formation theories. The new observations show it has only about five times more, making it far more similar to our own Jupiter. The discovery opens a new window into exoplanet atmospheres. The team has already found similar cloud cycles on two other hot Jupiters, WASP-39 b and WASP-17 b, and plans to expand the search. Understanding these extreme weather patterns could help us learn how planets form and evolve—and maybe even what to expect on worlds in other solar systems.
why_it_matters: This discovery reveals that weather on distant worlds can be far stranger than on Earth, and it shows how next-generation telescopes can untangle atmospheric details that challenge our understanding of planet formation.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST, launched in 2021) is the largest and most powerful space telescope ever built, designed to observe the universe in infrared light.
Hot Jupiters like WASP-94A b are gas giant planets that orbit extremely close to their parent stars—often much closer than Mercury is to our Sun—and were among the first exoplanets ever discovered.
Because WASP-94A b is tidally locked, the same hemisphere always faces its star, creating an extreme temperature difference between the permanent day side and the permanent night side.

Previous studies of exoplanet atmospheres using the Hubble Space Telescope (a smaller space observatory launched in 1990) were often blurred by cloud layers, but JWST's ability to isolate the morning and evening edges during a transit allows a much cleaner view.

The fact that the new data revised the planet's oxygen and carbon abundance down to about five times that of Jupiter, rather than hundreds of times, suggests that hot Jupiters may form more similarly to our own giant planets than previously thought.

perspectives.description: The direct observation of a cloud cycle on an exoplanet marks a major leap in astronomy. The ability to separate morning and evening sides solves past puzzles and offers a new toolkit for studying alien atmospheres with unprecedented clarity.

JWST time is limited, and focusing on hot Jupiters may divert resources from studying temperate, potentially habitable exoplanets. Also, the extreme conditions of these worlds make it hard to apply lessons to Earth-like planets.

Historically, the cloud problem has plagued spectroscopic studies of exoplanets since the first hot Jupiter atmospheres were examined in the early 2000s. This technique finally bypasses that barrier, marking a maturation of the field after decades of incremental progress.

The team plans to extend this analysis to many more hot Jupiters, and future observatories could apply similar methods to cooler, smaller exoplanets. Understanding these weather cycles may eventually inform what to expect on worlds in other solar systems.
